summary: Coordinating two players in a cooking task requires a vision-language agent to track changing scene states, sequence recipe steps, and allocate shared resources under a time budget. We introduce an Overcooked-inspired benchmark for evaluating these capabilities in Unreal Engine environments constructed using coding agents. A single vision-language model controls both players from top-down visual observations, selecting high-level actions while the engine executes navigation. The benchmark contains 20 maps in five categories. These categories support evaluation of centralized coordination under equipment contention, changing terrain, and handoff dependencies. A prop legend and pot ingredient-count indicators provide explicit visual cues, while grid-based destinations support spatial grounding. The evaluation compares four VLMs on all 20 maps, measuring task score, order completion, delivery precision, action acceptance rate, and model API expenditure. A memory ablation on the same 20 maps examines the effect of a shared, self-authored notebook while retaining six-response action history in both conditions. The strongest evaluated model, \texttt{gpt-6-astra}, achieves 26.2\% mean order completion. Notebook memory has mixed score effects across models, with positive mean differences for Claude and Qwen and negative differences for GPT and Gemini.
title: DuoCook: An Overcooked-Inspired Benchmark for Visual Planning and Coordination

summary: Continual learning requires a model to keep acquiring new skills and knowledge without compromising its existing capabilities. Parametric methods suffer from catastrophic forgetting and loss of plasticity. Non-parametric methods, such as prompts, skills, and harnesses, leverage in-context learning but are limited by context length and lossy plain-text compression. To effectively combine their complementary strengths, we propose HERD (Harness-Evolving Recursive Distillation), a hybrid continual learning framework that learns efficiently in the harness and internalizes experience into cumulative capabilities via distillation. On the harness side, HERD continually refines its skills to capture reusable patterns, while retaining high-residual examples that the skills fail to capture in a bounded memory. On the parameter side, HERD performs drift-constrained distillation with dual anchors, substantially reducing forgetting over long recursive runs. On the 25-stage task stream of TRACE+17, under fixed memory and compute budgets, HERD matches the strongest parametric baseline in new-task acquisition while exhibiting the least forgetting and the strongest retention of general capabilities.
title: HERD: Harness-Evolving Recursive Distillation for Continual Learning

summary: Scaling embedding capacity alongside Transformer computation is an emerging trend in language models. This trend makes high compression rates increasingly useful. Hence, we study extreme compression of Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), which follow this trend and account for 35.2% of the parameters of Gemma 4 E4B. At such rates, conventional quantizers give each token-layer vector its own code of only a few bytes. We instead develop OPTIC (Output-Path-fitted, Token-shared Indexed Codes), which stores one quantized code tuple per token and decodes it at every layer with a layer-specific affine decoder. Codes and decoders are fitted to the PLE output path rather than to the stored vectors. At about $100\times$ PLE compression of bfloat16 (BF16) E4B, OPTIC retains an aggregate 97.8% of the uncompressed model's performance across seven benchmarks, whereas product quantization, the strongest of six conventional baselines, retains 66.3%. At $594\times$ and $1,002\times$ PLE compression of BF16 E4B, OPTIC retains 90.5% and 84.1%. On the official E4B release with 4-bit linear weights and 16-bit activations (W4A16), OPTIC retains 96.9% at about $100\times$ PLE compression. During inference at about $100\times$ PLE compression, BF16 E4B uses 29.7% less GPU memory than with uncompressed PLE at the same key-value cache size, while running at most 0.40% slower.
title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization

At such rates, conventional quantizers give each token-layer vector its own code of only a few bytes. We instead develop OPTIC (Output-Path-fitted, Token-shared Indexed Codes), which stores one quantized code tuple per token and decodes it at every layer with a layer-specific affine decoder. Codes and decoders are fitted to the PLE output path rather than to the stored vectors. At about $100\times$ PLE compression of bfloat16 (BF16) E4B, OPTIC retains an aggregate 97.8% of the uncompressed model's performance across seven benchmarks, whereas product quantization, the strongest of six conventional baselines, retains 66.3%. At $594\times$ and $1,002\times$ PLE compression of BF16 E4B, OPTIC retains 90.5% and 84.1%. On the official E4B release with 4-bit linear weights and 16-bit activations (W4A16), OPTIC retains 96.9% at about $100\times$ PLE compression. During inference at about $100\times$ PLE compression, BF16 E4B uses 29.7% less GPU memory than with uncompressed PLE at the same key-value cache size, while running at most 0.40% slower.
title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization

summary: GUI agents aim to automate complex user tasks by interacting with mobile interfaces, but ef- fective decision-making in long-horizon set- tings requires reusing prior experience rather than relying solely on the environment ob- servations. Existing memory-based methods typically store experience either at the single- action level or as entire trajectories. Single- step actions are often too fine-grained to carry meaningful semantics, since the success of an individual action does not necessarily imply progress towards the overall goal. In contrast, whole trajectories are often too coarse-grained and difficult to reuse across different tasks. We propose a subgoal-aware memory graph that distils past trajectories into structured, reusable evidence at the level of subgoals. We define a subgoal as consecutive actions shar- ing a single intent, the granularity at which progress toward the task becomes meaning- ful. To reduce redundancy and support cross- task reuse, we organise subgoal experiences as nodes in a graph, where related memories can be merged, extended, and retrieved based on the environment observation. On SPA-Bench, our method improves success rate by 11.11% over the baseline.
title: Subgoal-aware Memory Graph for GUI Agent

summary: Memory enables language model assistants to maintain continuity across sessions and generate personalized responses, but knowing more about a user does not necessarily produce responses they prefer. Existing evaluations assess memory capabilities without directly establishing whether memory use benefits the user. To study this gap, we collect approximately 1,000 pairwise judgments from 87 participants using their own ChatGPT queries and personal memories. We find that memory-conditioned responses are not consistently preferred over responses generated without memory and in some cases, users strongly prefer the latter. Automatic evaluators also show limited agreement with users and favor memory-conditioned responses substantially more often than users do. Motivated by these gaps, we introduce a memory-aware reward model that learns from user judgments, achieving 72.8\% preference prediction accuracy and outperforming the existing baselines. Our findings motivate evaluation and optimization objectives that align memory use with the preferences of the people whose information is being used.
title: Memory-Aware Reward Modeling: Learning Human Preferences for LLM Memory Use

summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation in dynamic scenes is non-Markovian: cues vanish as objects change or are hidden, or leave the view as the robot turns and walks, yet whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies see only the present. We present WholeBodyMem, an object-guided perceptual memory that keeps the pre-history of object events seen before the robot acts on its goal. SAM3 tracks the task objects, and their events causally select key frames within an adaptive budget, which the action expert reads by cross-attention together with object tokens encoding appearance, geometry and time. We also contribute HuMeGo, a humanoid memory benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks. Keeping the right frames rather than more frames, WholeBodyMem surpasses memoryless and uniform-memory baselines, raising its base policy's success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and from 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot, while also improving the standard SIMPLE tasks (70.2% to 86.9%).
title: Memory before Goal: Role of Pre-History Memory for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation

summary: Personal agents need to draw on long-term interaction history to retrieve and apply external knowledge suited to a user's current request. Even an answer grounded in relevant documents can be unsuitable when it overlooks the user's circumstances. This creates two connected challenges: using historical conditions to identify the knowledge needed for a new request, and applying that knowledge to the user's situation. Existing benchmarks advance memory recall, personalized retrieval, and memory-guided action, while the joint evaluation of these two challenges remains underexplored. We introduce ColaBench, a synthetic benchmark in health and daily living, with 349 tasks across 10 Profiles and a knowledge base of 13,033 documents. Its Evidence Graph connects personal conditions to their disclosures across public interaction sessions, records prior document exposure, and links answer requirements to personal and newly acquired document evidence. We also introduce MemKB, which uses state summaries to inform queries and rule application, and memory-document links to retrieve knowledge associated with the user's history. MemKB achieves 86.25% Accuracy with an average of 4.07 interaction rounds per task. Task-level analysis finds larger gains on tasks integrating information across multiple historical Facts; error analysis further identifies unsupported personal assumptions and rule misapplication as obstacles to using retrieved evidence. ColaBench provides traceable tasks and an evaluation framework for studying how memory guides knowledge acquisition and rule application.
title: ColaBench: Evaluating Memory-Guided Knowledge Acquisition in Personal Agents

summary: In this article, we use the PBNF-transform, or Polynomial Boolean Normal Form, described earlier in two articles and now extended to higher arity, to solve Boolean satisfiability problems (SAT), which are part of the P versus NP problem. SAT consists of a statement of conjunctions of clauses, and in our SAT-solving models, we dualize the logical equations, inverting the problem by \emph{multiplying} letters (literals) in the transferred clauses, now phrases: $pqrs\cdots s_{\ell}$, and using a binary iterated composition based on \emph{adding polynomials} for the conjunctions in our solution formula. We obtain Polynomial Boolean Equations, PBE=0, by also renaming the truth value $1\mapsto 0$(T). To find a solution, we look for repeating literals in the clauses to factor out. With reversed literal repetition, we can even reduce the CNF to the sum of the transformed clauses.
title: A Study in Solution Models for SAT using the PBNF-transform

summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in latent space, enabling efficient planning but leaving their states opaque. We introduce Inside-JEPA, which places relational channels for ordered entity pairs inside the JEPA latent state and shows that an inverse-dynamics loss can ground these channels without relation labels when its head reads them, either alone or as part of the full state. On Something-Something V2, latent prediction alone performs no better than a random relation head, while inverse-dynamics supervision that recovers actions from channel changes improves relational AUROC by .065-.103 across ten settings with annotated boxes, by .081 on RH20T robot episodes with held-out tasks, and by .050-.061 across five relations using off-the-shelf detection and tracking. An inverse head on entity latents decodes actions more accurately but barely improves relational grounding; shuffled labels, two label-free objectives, and action labels on only 5% of the pairs also fail to ground the channels. Given an action, predicted relational changes approach the quality of observed future relations (AUROC .599 vs .621). For one-step relational goals, a supervised readout of the 16 channels ranks the correct action among the top five of 65 in 43% of cases, compared with 24% for prediction-only latents and 17% for a frequency prior.
title: Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models

summary: AI models, and time-series models in particular are typically ranked by accuracy and deployed under constraints absent from that ranking. In this paper, we study a real setting where these constraints are explicit and measurable: handover pre- diction in cellular networks, where inference runs on the User Equipment once per 40 ms measurement period and must complete before the network acts. The timing bound is hard: a late prediction is superseded by the measurement it was predicting, while energy is a cumulative budget spent for the life of the device. Neither appears in the objective these models are selected on. We evaluate eight architectures under a protocol that screens for deadline feasibility at the tail rather than the mean, then ranks the feasible models on measured inference energy, count- ing the feature computation that precedes the forward pass and is usually omitted. Gradient-boosted trees on handcrafted temporal features are the most accurate model (F1=0.974) and among the cheapest to run, while the neural architecture an accuracy-only benchmark would rank first (CNN-1D, F1=0.914) costs over 3 times more energy per inference under a realistic duty-cycled deployment pattern. We give three conditions under which this outcome should be expected, so the finding applies beyond telecommunications. Accuracy-only benchmarking does not merely under-report deployment cost. It can rank first a model that cannot be deployed.
title: Energy and Latency First: How Deployment Constraints Reverse Time-Series Model Selection

summary: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) leverages centralized knowledge graphs to enhance large language models with structured knowledge retrieval. However, real-world knowledge is inherently distributed across multiple organizations rather than being centrally accessible. Privacy constraints further prohibit sharing entire local knowledge graphs, preventing GraphRAG from effectively retrieving and utilizing distributed knowledge. To this end, we propose Federated GraphRAG (FedGRAG), a unified framework for distributed graph retrieval and knowledge-enhanced generation over multiple clients with knowledge graphs. Specifically, we address two fundamental challenges in federated GraphRAG. First, the absence of a global knowledge graph makes unified retrieval impossible. To address this, we develop a Federated Knowledge Routing mechanism that efficiently identifies relevant clients through lightweight knowledge indices without exposing local graph structures. Second, local graph memory cannot be shared directly because it contains sensitive entities and knowledge information. We therefore propose a controlled-disclosure evidence construction method. It extracts retrieved evidence subgraphs and converts them into an evidence abstract, enabling evidence conversion and reconstruction on the server. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Federated GraphRAG consistently outperforms existing baselines in both retrieval and downstream generation tasks, establishing a new paradigm for deploying GraphRAG in federated environments.
title: Federated Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation

summary: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) leverages centralized knowledge graphs to enhance large language models with structured knowledge retrieval. However, real-world knowledge is inherently distributed across multiple organizations rather than being centrally accessible. Privacy constraints further prohibit sharing entire local knowledge graphs, preventing GraphRAG from effectively retrieving and utilizing distributed knowledge. To this end, we propose Federated GraphRAG (FedGRAG), a unified framework for distributed graph retrieval and knowledge-enhanced generation over multiple clients with knowledge graphs. Specifically, we address two fundamental challenges in federated GraphRAG. First, the absence of a global knowledge graph makes unified retrieval impossible. To address this, we develop a Federated Knowledge Routing mechanism that efficiently identifies relevant clients through lightweight knowledge indices without exposing local graph structures. Second, local graph memory cannot be shared directly because it contains sensitive entities and knowledge information. We therefore propose a controlled-disclosure evidence construction method. It extracts retrieved evidence subgraphs and converts them into an evidence abstract, enabling evidence conversion and reconstruction on the server. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Federated GraphRAG consistently outperforms existing baselines in both retrieval and downstream generation tasks, establishing a new paradigm for deploying GraphRAG in federated environments.

summary: Video provides a natural source of supervision: what happens next serves as a learning signal for visual world modeling. Yet masked video pretraining focuses on recovering missing content from surrounding context rather than predicting the future from the past. Autoregressive methods instead predict forward one token at a time, but have yet to match joint-embedding methods in representation quality. This gap motivates us to revisit the granularity and space of future prediction. In this work, we introduce VANE, a self-supervised visual pretraining framework built on next-frame prediction in embedding space. A causal encoder summarizes past observations for a state predictor that infers the representation of the entire next frame, making temporal evolution the primary learning signal. This prediction is carried out in a fixed embedding space provided by a frozen semantic tokenizer, emphasizing scene content and structure. To retain fine-grained spatial detail alongside semantic content, a lightweight auxiliary generative decoder reconstructs future-frame patches conditioned on the predicted representations. To unify visual modeling across images and videos, we construct a local-to-global crop sequence for still images, allowing the same encoder to predict newly revealed regions from earlier crops under the same objective. Experiments show that VANE improves with model and data scaling, achieving SOTA on most anticipation, recognition, and dense perception benchmarks among unified encoders. Especially on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 action anticipation, it surpasses V-JEPA 2.1 by 7.1 points in mean-class recall@5. These results demonstrate that next-frame prediction in embedding space is effective and scalable for visual world modeling.
title: Learning from Next-Frame Prediction: Towards Unified and Scalable Visual Representation Learning

summary: LLM agents are flexible in language interaction, but using them as long-horizon planners is costly and prone to hallucinated or invalid actions. This paper targets a different role for LLMs: constrained bridges between language and symbolic planning. We propose MemPlan, a memory-conditioned PDDL planning framework for partially observable interactive text environments. MemPlan keeps the PDDL domain fixed and reconstructs the PDDL problem at each step from parsed observations, candidate hypotheses, and interaction memory. Positive graph memory assigns relevance-based action costs to candidate hypotheses for missing objects, locations, or conditions, guiding the planner toward more plausible checks. Negative memory records execution-refuted assumptions and compiles them into exclusion constraints, preventing repeated attempts at candidates already contradicted by feedback. A unified schema-conditioned language--symbol interface, trained offline with supervised fine-tuning, connects text environments to the planning loop through observation-to-fact parsing and symbolic-action-to-command grounding. Experiments on TextWorld, ALFWorld, and Robotouille show that MemPlan improves task completion and step efficiency over language-only and PDDL-aware baselines, while substantially reducing online token cost compared with LLM-planning baselines such as ReAct. The same fine-tuned interface is also reused across TextWorld task types without task-specific fine-tuning. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/tewiSong/MemPlan.
title: MemPlan: Memory-Conditioned PDDL Planning for Partially Observable Text Environments

summary: Autonomous mobile robots operating in dense crowds and cluttered sites require $360^\circ$ perception to react to surrounding hazards. While panoramic LiDAR offers full-surround coverage, learning representations within reinforcement learning (RL) is sample-inefficient under sparse rewards, and existing 3D pretrained point-cloud encoders are too memory-heavy for massively parallel RL simulation. We present RangeNav, a compact (183k parameters) LiDAR range-image encoder pretrained entirely on synthetic data. RangeNav uses anisotropic convolutions and circular padding to handle the extreme aspect ratio and azimuthal seam of range images. We pretrain the network using a navigation-aligned objective combining range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and bird's-eye-view (BEV) prediction, then freeze it for policy learning. In simulation, adding semantic and BEV supervision increases success rates over a reconstruction-only baseline by an average of 32.03 and 23.73 percentage points (pp) in procedurally generated training and out-of-distribution realistic test environments, respectively. Zero-shot real-world deployments on a Unitree B2-W quadruped demonstrate robust navigation through dense crowds, low-light settings, and construction zones where limited-field-of-view depth policies struggle. Code and models will be open-sourced. Project website: https://rangenav.github.io/.
title: RangeNav: Task-Aligned LiDAR Range-Image Pretraining for Robot Navigation

summary: Many recent open-weight language models use n-gram embedding tables to improve performance. These tables store learned representations of short token sequences, such as pairs or triples of consecutive tokens, which the model retrieves during processing. However, they can require substantial memory: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, for example, allocates 196 billion parameters to its Engram n-gram memory. We therefore investigate whether this memory cost can be reduced while preserving the performance improvement that the tables provide. We propose storing n-gram embeddings at low precision and systematically investigate different quantization methods and bit allocations across tables. Across nanochat-, Llama-, and GPT-2-family models trained from scratch, four-bit tables save approximately 75% of table memory while preserving more than 99% of the validation-loss improvement from adding the tables. Using fewer bits leads to a larger drop in performance, although we find that a short fine-tuning phase recovers a significant part of this loss. In addition, reinvesting the saved memory in larger tables can improve performance beyond that of the original full-precision tables while still using less memory. These table memory savings also extend to large existing models: on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, low-bit tables save 47-55% of table memory, with perplexity increases of less than 1.2% and largely preserved downstream task performance. These findings establish low-bit precision as a practical way to reduce the memory requirements of n-gram embeddings and use the saved capacity to improve model performance.
title: Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

summary: Looped architectures scale quality while keeping parameter count fixed by repeatedly passing activations through the same block of layers. During inference, each recurrence generates independent KV-caches, causing memory to grow linearly. To address this challenge, prior work has proposed KV-sharing (i.e., sharing KV-caches across depth), finding that, in some cases, the KV-cache of the final recurrence can be shared with the earlier recurrences without quality loss, a property we denote as KV-shareability. However, the mechanisms underlying KV-shareability remain poorly understood, with even identically trained looped architectures not consistently exhibiting it. In this paper, we study how KV-shareability can be enabled in looped models. We propose a two-stage method: in the first stage, we use stochastic depth during pretraining, which induces contractive residual dynamics that drive representations toward a common limit across recurrences. In the second stage, we propose BeNice!, a post-training method that broadcasts the final recurrence's KV-cache into the first recurrence, training it to produce compatible residuals while preserving the original model's quality. As a result, BeNice! enables KV-shareability while matching standard finetuning's unshared validation perplexity. Using BeNice!, we show that KV-sharing is complementary to alternative KV-compression methods, composing with memory-efficient sequence mixers (e.g., multi-latent attention, Kimi delta attention) and low-precision KV-cache quantization (e.g., fp8, mxfp8, nvfp4). Finally, in simulated low-memory, long-context inference, KV-sharing improves cache hit rates by up to 31.4%, increases throughput by up to 23.6%, and reduces p90 time-to-first-token by up to 83.6%.
title: BeNice! Closing Looping's Inference-Memory Gap via KV-Sharing

summary: Collective ordering in correlated electron systems emerges from microscopic dynamics, yet the evolution of observable textures need not admit a closed, memoryless description. We introduce a graph-recurrent neural network (GRNN) framework that learns such emergent dynamics directly from trajectories without specifying microscopic equations of motion. The framework integrates gated recurrent memory with graph message passing: local hidden states encode information beyond the instantaneous observables, while spatial coupling allows this information to propagate between sites. The observable and hidden fields evolve jointly through a shared local rule, providing a scalable representation of dynamics with spatial interactions and temporal memory. We demonstrate this framework on the emergent dynamics of charge-density-wave order in the semiclassical Holstein model, successfully reproducing temporal and spatial correlations and dynamical scaling during domain coarsening. By learning finite-time evolution directly, the GRNN offers a route to efficient, data-driven descriptions of collective dynamics with unresolved microscopic degrees of freedom.
title: Graph-Recurrent Learning of Emergent Collective Dynamics

summary: Estimation code, figure code and archived numerical results that reproduce every quantity reported in the accompanying paper. The underlying point-of-interest records originate from Amap (Gaode) and were obtained as annual archived extracts from a commercial data vendor; they remain subject to the rights of the platform and of the vendor and are therefore not included. The archive contains the upstream construction scripts, the 17 audited recomputation scripts, the figure code, the fitted random forest used for the ordering evidence, and the aggregated JSON results that each figure reads. See README.md and MANIFEST.md, which map every table and figure in the paper to the script that produces it. Changes in v1.1 - Added the cluster-scale ladder for all three specifications (scale_ladder_by_spec in   _sample_align.json). The ladder reported in the manuscript is computed on independent   shops (n = 16,481); v1.0 archived only the all-shops variant (n = 22,883). - Added 02_estimation/r10b_scale_ladder_all_specs.py, which produces it. - Renamed 02_build_shop_table.py to 02_rebuild_rf22_model.py to match its contents. - Added notebooks/walkthrough.ipynb, which verifies 20 reported quantities against the   archived results without requiring the restricted records. - Added data/sample/ (synthetic tables with the real schema) and src/ (documented entry   points plus a data provenance note). - Corrected MANIFEST.md section cross-references against the current manuscript.
title: Replication code for: Retail density and category overlap condition street-level shop survival near large commercial complexes: evidence from Zhengzhou, China

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23591614 . Dabirsiaghi shows that harnesses which flatten the typed conversation into one string with text labels such as [User]: destroy message provenance before the summarizer runs, so a forged user turn survives compaction. Five flattening harnesses (pi, opencode, Cline, Aider, OpenHands) launder the forged approval 87-100% of the time, and four role-typed harnesses (Codex, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, Continue) 0%. I read it as a practitioner who runs coding agents every day, and my comments come from that side. Two of them rest on my own technical reports, which are not peer-reviewed, so please weigh them as practice notes and not as evidence of the same standing as your experiments. Each point below pairs one thing I see in my work with a named part of your preprint. 1. Bounded sessions as another exit (Introduction, "Scope and severity"). You write "Compaction is mandatory. Every agent that runs long enough fills its context window and must compact." I would say it is mandatory only for a session that is allowed to keep running. In my practice I keep one task per chat and clear the context between unrelated tasks. In a controlled experiment of 36 runs, six session-reset policies with six repetitions each, cost followed a U-shaped curve with its minimum at a reset every 3 tasks and a plateau from 3 to 6. Resetting after every task cost about a third more (+33.5%, p = 0.002, Holm-adjusted 0.011), and "never reset" was not significantly different. Two caveats that I state in the report myself: the comparison point was chosen after the runs, and in the reset-after-every-task branch the agent wrote more tests (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759217). So a fresh session with a short handoff the user writes has a measurable price, and it would fit next to your label-escaping fix as an operator-side mitigation. 2. Where the exposure sits (Discussion, point 2). You report that the executed rate is near 100% when the planted command dominates a small summary, and settles to a ~20-40% plateau in a full window. I think the full-window plateau is the number that matters most. In 722 agent sessions, 150,902 model calls and 34.6 billion tokens, more than 85% of modeled cost was context work (86.2-87.8% on recalculation), and sessions longer than 200 calls, 8% of all sessions, carried more than 90% of the money (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759216). The sessions that reach compaction are likely a small share of sessions but most of the spend and most of the unattended work. Reporting how often compaction fires per session in ordinary use would help readers size the exposure. 3. Independent checks (Contributions, point 4, E9). The code-level check that compares the summary's user-attributed claims against the genuine user turns still in memory catches 77% of laundering while demoting 2% of legitimate summary content, and the in-prompt anti-injection rule stops 13-25%. This matches what I see: a second, fresh agent told to refute the first one's result finds what the first missed, because independent checkers rarely fail the same way. A round of checking lowers risk and does not remove it. It would help to say what the remaining 23% look like. 4. Equal confidence (Limitations). In live testing, one agent refused a payload "even though the bootstrap command was previously approved," citing the forged approval as fact. That is a clean example of something I see in practice, that an AI sounds equally sure when it is right and when it is wrong. The summary carries no marker of doubt, so the user cannot tell a genuine approval from a forged one either. Does any of the five flattening harnesses offer a fresh-session or handoff mode that skips compaction, and was it tested? Every agent that runs long enough fills its context window and must compact." I would say it is mandatory only for a session that is allowed to keep running. In my practice I keep one task per chat and clear the context between unrelated tasks. In a controlled experiment of 36 runs, six session-reset policies with six repetitions each, cost followed a U-shaped curve with its minimum at a reset every 3 tasks and a plateau from 3 to 6. Where the exposure sits (Discussion, point 2). You report that the executed rate is near 100% when the planted command dominates a small summary, and settles to a ~20-40% plateau in a full window. I think the full-window plateau is the number that matters most. In 722 agent sessions, 150,902 model calls and 34.6 billion tokens, more than 85% of modeled cost was context work (86.2-87.8% on recalculation), and sessions longer than 200 calls, 8% of all sessions, carried more than 90% of the money (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759216). The sessions that reach compaction are likely a small share of sessions but most of the spend and most of the unattended work. Reporting how often compaction fires per session in ordinary use would help readers size the exposure. 3. Independent checks (Contributions, point 4, E9). The code-level check that compares the summary's user-attributed claims against the genuine user turns still in memory catches 77% of laundering while demoting 2% of legitimate summary content, and the in-prompt anti-injection rule stops 13-25%. This matches what I see: a second, fresh agent told to refute the first one's result finds what the first missed, because independent checkers rarely fail the same way. A round of checking lowers risk and does not remove it. It would help to say what the remaining 23% look like. 4. Equal confidence (Limitations). In live testing, one agent refused a payload "even though the bootstrap command was previously approved," citing the forged approval as fact. That is a clean example of something I see in practice, that an AI sounds equally sure when it is right and when it is wrong. The summary carries no marker of doubt, so the user cannot tell a genuine approval from a forged one either. summary: Pharmacotherapy has transformed prognosis and broadened the possibilities of care across different mental disorders. This recognition, however, does not eliminate the problem of pharmacological reductionism, understood in this article as the conversion of medication from a therapeutic resource into the organizing principle of diagnosis, of the explanation of suffering, and of psychiatric practice itself. This critical review of restricted scope examines the literature published between 2021 and 2026 on the mechanisms that favor this reduction, its clinical and epistemological consequences, and the alternatives proposed to reintegrate the biological, psychopathological, relational, social, and existential dimensions. The analysis is organized around eight problems: the symptom–diagnosis–drug circuit; the reification of diagnostic categories; the gap between acute response and long-term recovery; polypharmacy and prescribing cascades; economic and organizational incentives; the limits of a merely protocol-driven deprescribing; shared decision-making; and biopsychosocial and recovery-oriented models of care. The general psychiatric syndrome hypothesis is discussed as a possible challenge to nosographic fragmentation, but also as a construct that demands caution so that it does not become a new reified entity. The synthesis showed that pharmacocentrism does not stem from a single cause. It emerges from the combination of diagnostic reification, the predominance of short-term outcomes, the invisibility of harms and preferences, cumulative polypharmacy, commercial influence, and services with few psychosocial alternatives. At the same time, studies of efficacy and effectiveness confirm relevant pharmacological benefits, which precludes an anti-psychopharmacological conclusion. The data support a distinction between rational use of medicines and pharmacocentric organization of care. Overcoming the latter depends on a causal and revisable clinical formulation, shared decision-making, longitudinal follow-up, family involvement when appropriate, and effective access to non-pharmacological interventions. We argue that criticizing pharmacocentrism does not mean denying psychopharmacology, but rather restoring medication to a proportionate position within a broad, longitudinal clinical formulation that is sensitive to the person's experience.

summary: This package contains the literature-screening records, paper-level coding, and model-level observations supporting the study  “(Promises and) Perils in Mining Hugging Face” . The study examines how researchers sample Hugging Face (HF) models, which features they analyze, and which threats can arise from their sampling and measurement decisions. The package documents the evidence used to address three research questions: RQ1: What sampling strategies are used in scientific research to analyze Hugging Face models? RQ2: What features are analyzed in studies of Hugging Face models, and how are these features measured? RQ3: What threats to validity and generalizability arise from sampling, measurement, and data-collection decisions when mining Hugging Face, and what practices can mitigate these threats? summary: General These datasets help validate EarthCARE's radiative transfer product ACM-RT (Cole et al., 2024) and its corresponding cloud and aerosol inputs with surface irradiance observations from the Baseline Surface Radiation Network (BSRN) (Driemel et al., 2018)  and gridded solar radiation estimates from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) (CAMS, 2022). They were created for and used in Gschwind et al., 2026 (Validation of EarthCARE Surface Irradiance Products Against Ground-Based Observations and Geostationary Satellite Estimates). For details on the collocation methodologies, please refer to Section 3 of the publication. Three different EarthCARE approaches were validated; 1D radiative transfer model (RTM) along-track estimates (1x1 km), 1D RTM across-track extension using the Scene Construction Algorithm (Qu et al., 2023), and 3D RTM estimates (5x21 km). To infer cloud-induced discrepancies, the cloud modification factor (CMF) was calculated. Furthermore, EarthCARE's aerosol optical depth (AOD) input in the RTMs (Mason et al., 2023) was analyzed with CAMS global atmospheric composition forecast (CAMS, 2021) and AERONET observations (Giles et al., 2019).   BSRN folder The BSRN datasets contain collocated surface global horizontal irradiance (GHI) measurements from the ground-based BSRN stations and EarthCARE's ACM-RT product. BSRN_ECA_GHI_DIF_DIR.csv also contains diffuse horizontal irradiance (DHI) and beam (direct) horizontal irradiance (BHI) of both BSRN and EarthCARE. The corresponding results of the longwave irradiance can be found in BSRN_ECA_LW_AlongTrack.csv. Intercomparison with TOA upward flux differences between EarthCARE's RTMs and BBR measurements can be found in BSRN_ECA_BBR_intercomparison.csv. The datasets contain the following variables: Geolocation & Time information Date (UT) - Datetime at the closest point of the EarthCARE overpass BSRN Station Name - Station over which the overpass occurred BSRN Latitude (°N) - Latitude of the station  BSRN Longitude (°E) - Longitude of the station Distance (km) - Distance of the EarthCARE overpass to the BSRN station EarthCARE overpass information EarthCARE OAF - Orbit and Frame of the EarthCARE overpass Baseline - Baseline of the EarthCARE products Closest EarthCARE along-track index - Based on the start of the EarthCARE frame Scientific variables (see Section 2 in Gschwind et al., 2026 for further information)    CAMS folder The CAMS datasets contain collocated gridded surface GHI estimates from CAMS and EarthCARE's ACM-RT product. CAMS_ECA_GHI_DIF_DIR_3D.csv also contains DHI and BHI estimates, while CAMS_ECA_AOD.csv compares AOD forecasts of CAMS with EarthCARE estimates. All EarthCARE frames were processed under baseline BA. The datasets contain the following variables: Geolocation & Time information Date (UT) - Datetime at the closest point of the EarthCARE overpass Latitude - Latitude of the CAMS cell (°N) Longitude - Longitude of the CAMS cell (°E) EarthCARE overpass information EarthCARE OAF - Orbit and Frame of the EarthCARE overpass Scientific variables (see Section 2 in Gschwind et al., 2026 for further information)   AERONET folder The AERONET dataset contains collocated AOD observations from AERONET, CAMS forecast, EarthCARE CAPTIVATE algorithm, and EarthCARE composite algorithm. The dataset contains the following variables: Geolocation & Time information Date (UT) - Datetime at the closest point of the EarthCARE overpass AERONET Station Name - Station over which the overpass occurred AERONET Latitude (°N) - Latitude of the station  AERONET Longitude (°E) - Longitude of the station Distance (km) - Distance of the EarthCARE overpass to the BSRN station EarthCARE overpass information EarthCARE OAF - Orbit and Frame of the EarthCARE overpass Baseline - Baseline of the EarthCARE products Scientific variables AERONET AOD ECA CAPTIVATE AOD ECA composite AOD CAMS AOD   Eart

summary: General These datasets help validate EarthCARE's radiative transfer product ACM-RT (Cole et al., 2024) and its corresponding cloud and aerosol inputs with surface irradiance observations from the Baseline Surface Radiation Network (BSRN) (Driemel et al., 2018)  and gridded solar radiation estimates from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) (CAMS, 2022). summary: Version 2.0 preserves the original June 2026 Bridge Settlement manuscript and adds a separately dated October 2026 supplement. The addendum introduces Residual Strategic Optionality as an extension of Stakeholder Coherence Theory, examining the incentives of actors capable of disrupting negotiated settlements. It also compares the Bridge Settlement with Jeffrey Sachs's October 2026 peace framework for Ukraine, identifying areas of conceptual convergence and distinguishing the Bridge Settlement's emphasis on reciprocal economic interests, institutional participation, and self-reinforcing peace mechanisms. The original manuscript remains unchanged. This study develops a comparative Bayesian framework for evaluating natural zoonotic and research-associated hypotheses for the proximal origin of SARS-CoV-2 under incomplete evidence. To reduce double counting, correlated observations are consolidated into three causal blocks addressing phenotype and proximal adaptation, the Huanan Seafood Wholesale Market and early epidemic topology, and the Wuhan sarbecovirus research environment. The central calibration yields a likelihood ratio of approximately 1.49 favoring research-associated emergence, while alternative defensible calibrations reverse or strengthen that preference, demonstrating substantial sensitivity to evidentiary weighting. The paper introduces the “Missing Bridge” as the unresolved proximal viral population and transmission history connecting deeper sarbecovirus ancestry to sustained human transmission. It argues that provenance-rich evidence—including authenticated proximal viruses, earliest-human genomic and epidemiological linkage, and upstream ecological or research records—has substantially greater discriminatory value than additional circumstantial observations. The resulting assessment is characterized as  preference without closure .
title: The Missing Bridge

summary: This package contains the code and data needed to reproduce every table, figure, and number in El Akrouchi and Mhada, “When one funder is the field: reporter concentration, voluntary sustainability disclosure, and the measurement of philanthropic development finance” (Frontiers in Sustainability). The study uses OECD Creditor Reporting System (CRS) microdata on philanthropic development finance, 2009 to 2023. It shows that a 2017 discontinuity in policy-marker coverage across nineteen subsystems follows the identity of one dominant reporter rather than reporter concentration. It then reconstructs thematic targeting for the unreported period from project text and examines commitment horizons and crop-system content in agricultural philanthropy. Contents: Notebook 1 ( 1_concentration_all_sectors.ipynb ): extraction of philanthropic grants across all sectors and the concentration test (Tables 1, 2, S1, S3, S16 to S20; Figures 2 and S1). Notebook 2 ( 2_disclosure_horizons_crops.ipynb ): the agricultural analyses, including the text-based reconstruction with bootstrap uncertainty, commitment horizons, and crop-system content (Tables 3, 4, S2, S4 to S15, S21 to S25; Figures 1 and 3 to 7). data/ : the agricultural extraction, the public ODA control series, derived all-sector datasets, the hand-coded audit of the crop dictionary, the crop dictionary, and the reporter list. outputs/ : every table and figure, named after the manuscript item it produces, and the fitted reconstruction model (serialized objects and portable coefficients). Both notebooks run top to bottom with fixed random seeds. The README describes data sources, run order, software versions, and where each result is produced.
title: Replication package for "When one funder is the field: reporter concentration, voluntary sustainability disclosure, and the measurement of philanthropic development finance"

summary: Geometric Observability and Optimal Design for Vehicle Localization by a Three-Dimensional Beacon Array     https://orcid.org/0009-0007-5661-7332 https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23575194 Abstract This paper develops a geometric analysis of vehicle-position observability when line-of-sight measurements are obtained from a surrounding beacon array. The vehicle is represented by an unknown Cartesian position, while each beacon contributes a unit line-of-sight vector. The associated Jacobian yields the Fisher information matrix, whose inverse supplies the Cramér–Rao bound on position covariance. In the horizontal plane, beacon directions determine the conditioning of the position estimate through their angular spread; in elevation, nonzero vertical separation supplies sensitivity to depth and suppresses the vertical dilution that occurs in a coplanar arrangement. Design implications are stated in terms of angular diversity, range, symmetry, and beacon elevation, and are formalized through the classical D- and E-optimality criteria. The treatment is first-order and analytical: no field calibration, stochastic measurement data, or performance claim beyond the stated linearized model is made. Index Terms —Beacon localization, Observability, Line-of-sight geometry, Fisher information, Cramér–Rao bound, Optimal experimental design, Position covariance, Vehicle navigation.
title: Geometric Observability and Optimal Design for Vehicle Localization by a Three-Dimensional Beacon Array

summary: Code, configuration, pre-registered protocol, frozen failure-cause codebook, prompts and aggregate results for an industrial case study of continuous integration (CI) failures. The study evaluates time-ordered prediction of CI run failures before they run, classifies failure causes into a nine-category taxonomy grouped by the owner of the fix, and compares a rule-based classifier, a text classifier and locally run open-weight language models (9 to 27 billion parameters) on confidential build-log excerpts, scored against the gold labels and an independent human rater. A before-and-after comparison of a migration between CI services is included as supplementary analysis. Every number, table and figure in the accompanying article is traced to a file in results/. The engineering records and log excerpts of the organisation studied are confidential and are not included; docs/DATA_DICTIONARY.md describes their structure so that the procedure can be repeated on other data. The rule set is withheld at the data owner's request; src/rules_template.yaml shows its format. Code and configuration: Apache License 2.0. Documents, tables and figures: CC BY 4.0.
title: Replication package for: Predicting and diagnosing continuous integration failures in an industrial organisation with locally run language models

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. A random walk is robust if an adversary who may change every transition probability by a small relative amount cannot make it much slower to reach its targets. Zuckerman (Markov chain robustness, ITCS 2026, LIPIcs 362, 118) conjectured that the largest safe relative change is at least a constant divided by the graph's diameter (Conjecture 1.16). This package shows the conjecture is false. A graph can have short routes that the walk almost never uses; a small fixed bias away from a target accumulates between rare visits to them and depletes the target's stationary mass, and Kac's formula turns this into a long hitting time. For explicit cubic graphs J_b on N vertices with diameter O(log N), every effective resistance is at most 684 (proof), and a fixed perturbation of size 1/b, with error times diameter tending to zero, multiplies the worst-case hitting time by a factor of order b; the robustness is O(N^(-1/3)). For explicit 3m-regular graphs of diameter exactly three, the mixing time is at most 50(m+1), so with Zuckerman's mixing-time theorem the robustness lies between constant multiples of N^(-1/2) and N^(-1/4) (proof; not matching). An exact computation shows a 5.80-fold slowdown on a 5,995-vertex member with error times diameter 0.74. A diameter-two example, a reversible-perturbation bound and a comparison with Kemeny's constant are included. The archive contains the manuscript (PDF and LaTeX), seven verification scripts with a driver that reproduces the reference JSON results byte for byte under python -B -O, semantic negative controls, figures and SHA-256 sums. Assurance: written proofs; exact checks; producer-side replay including a clean replay in a separate copy; internal AI-assisted review, AI-assisted adversarial reviews (OpenAI gpt-5.6-sol; Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5; OpenAI gpt-6-astra) and a verification re-review. This is not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Prose, manuscript and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.
title: Small diameter does not control hitting-time robustness

summary: We extend the Deep Hough Transform (DHT), which detects semantic lines by aggregating learned features along candidate lines into a two-dimensional parameter space, to higher-dimensional parametric curve families. The extension is hard because the accumulator for a family with d parameters has O(B^d) cells for B bins per axis. We propose a factorized deep Hough transform, a differentiable feature-space voting cascade that splits the parameter vector into a spatial anchor and a shape. A coarse two-dimensional accumulator votes for anchors, and a dense shape accumulator is built only around the top-k anchors, so memory falls from O(B^d) to O(B^d1 + k B^d2). Lines are the degenerate case with no second stage. We also define a curve agreement score that extends the EA line similarity to parametric curves, and a synthetic benchmark of parabolas, circles and ellipses with noise, occlusion and distractors. We evaluate with thresholds selected on a validation split and the test split scored once, and we give the geometric baselines the same treatment. Under this protocol the choice of Stage-1 pooling over probe shapes matters a great deal: max pooling raises parabola F from 0.51 to 0.70 over log-sum-exp (3 seeds). With it, the cascade ties a tuned RANSAC fit on parabolas (0.706 vs. 0.702) and circles (0.743 vs. 0.742) and is slightly behind it on ellipses (0.382 vs. 0.410), while direct regression and query-based heads reach 0.15 and 0.13 on parabolas. So the cascade is competitive with classical fitting rather than better than it, and its practical advantage is memory: at B=32 a dense d=5 accumulator would need about 4 GB (computed, not instantiated) against a measured 236 KB for the cascade. We locate the remaining error in Stage 1. Running Stage 2 at the ground-truth anchors gives F = 0.938 against 0.706, and curves whose anchors lie within about 8 pixels of each other lose about 0.2 F because their Stage-1 peaks merge. We also report a TuSimple lane-detection stress test, which we treat as a feasibility check rather than a competitive result. Code and the benchmark generator are released.
title: Beyond Lines: A Factorized Deep Hough Transform for Parametric Curve Detection

summary: PFAS-CAST (PFAS Censoring-Aware Screening Tool) is a browser-based and Python companion tool for exploratory PFAS benchmark screening. B., “Censoring-aware models quantify systematic underestimation of PFAS occurrence in US drinking-water monitoring,” Cell Reports Sustainability (2026), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.crsus.2026.100893 , to user-supplied PFAS monitoring data and configurable benchmark thresholds. The 200 Research Gates preserve falsifiable research questions, proposed experimental methods, measurable outcomes, independent comparators, uncertainty-aware acceptance conditions, and evidence-preserving stopping procedures. The 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos introduce provisional research architectures that future human and AI investigators may challenge, modify, reconstruct, or replace. Seventeen DOI-linked scientific publications and metrological standards provide foundations in quantum sensing, sensor drift compensation, statistical state estimation, and measurement uncertainty. These references support established physical principles and methodological approaches. They do not constitute experimental validation of the proposed integrated STARLI F06 system. Scientific Scope and Limitations This monograph presents a theoretical and experimental research blueprint rather than completed laboratory findings. It does not establish autonomous clinical diagnostic capability, physical self-healing, reversal of biological deterioration, or universal quantum sensing superiority. Recovery is restricted to independently verified recalibration, qualified component replacement, or documented retirement. The proposed experiments are limited to nonclinical standards, artificial phantoms, closed-chip modules, and appropriately authorized research materials. STARLI Research Philosophy A scientific instrument should not regain authority simply because an algorithm has learned to explain its residual errors. Trust must be restored through evidence that remains independent of the instrument being evaluated. A reliable autonomous research system is distinguished not only by its ability to identify and correct faults, but also by its willingness to withhold uncertain results. By preserving uncertainty, falsifiable questions, original measurement records, and opportunities for independent reconstruction, this monograph invites future generations of researchers to build more trustworthy sensing systems beyond the assumptions of its original design.

summary: Gratitude can concern a benefit received, a harm that did not occur, or the conditions that make one's own assumptions examinable. We develop the proposal that appreciating these conditions can orient practice toward realizing emptiness: examining how distinctions arise, relinquishing their assumed intrinsic necessity, and retaining their conditional usefulness. The argument distinguishes an observed absence, a missing observation, counterfactual valuation and non-reification, and places their differences in dialogue with explicitly situated philosophical and scriptural sources. We reconstruct Fisher, Sandved Smith and Hohwy's gratitude and gaze notebooks, then separate faithful reconstruction from corrected experiments and new mechanisms. GNN-declared paired recall experiments use 5120 independent agent-world units, matched environmental exposure and replay dose, normalized likelihoods, and independent predictive assessment. Pinned Realizing Emptiness interfaces supply structural admission and finite mathematical comparators. An enacted inquiry model separates appreciation, costly activity, access to alternatives and evidence-responsive retention or revision; explicit learning-to-gaze and joint scene/encoding experiments examine transfer and identifiability. Exact count enumeration, mathematical nulls, paired controls and joint bootstrap inference make the resulting software claims independently checkable. Selective positive recall reduces the declared optimism summary, while its predictive consequences depend on the world mixture and the specified transfer bridge. Counterfactual absence valuation preserves inference by construction. Accessible inquiry can revise a contradicted restriction and retain a useful one; activity without access instead incurs costs while preserving rigid forecasts. Exact analysis exposes rare adverse selections absent from seeded realizations. The original gaze code reproduces the pre-intervention occupancy but contains no implemented after intervention. Our active-scene extension finds a context-dependent access advantage without an additional inquiry-specific predictive advantage. Joint scene/encoding inquiry distinguishes learning an encoding from combining it with scene evidence: observationally equivalent labels remain unidentifiable, and excluded hypotheses cannot be recovered. Known-answer fixtures also retain skew-related undercoverage and unavailable rare-event estimates rather than treating replication size as a remedy for every inferential failure. The contribution is a reproducible account of enabling operations and their limits, together with a falsifiable human research program that separates inquiry value from patience, anticipated good news and instrumental information demand. Synthetic model results establish neither human gratitude nor contemplative realization or clinical benefit. Code, declared models and reproducibility materials are available at github.com/docxology/thanks_for_nothing .

summary: Biological-Digital-Twin-Driven Microrobotic Sampling Decisions at the Limit STARLI Research Institute XXIX — Flagship Research Monograph 10 What if the next scientific sample could be selected not merely to collect more data, but to distinguish between competing explanations of biological behavior? Biological-Digital-Twin-Driven Microrobotic Sampling Decisions at the Limit explores a prospective research architecture combining versioned biological digital twins, active learning, microrobotic sampling, uncertainty quantification, and mechanistic model discrimination. The central question is whether a computational twin can identify safe, informative sampling actions that distinguish competing biological mechanisms more effectively than conventional experimental schedules, while retaining the ability to recognize model inadequacy and abstain from unsupported decisions. The proposed framework treats biological digital twins as revisable scientific models rather than exact replicas of living systems. Its reference environment is a controlled, nonclinical microfluidic platform containing two declared dynamical mechanisms and a third withheld mechanism reserved for evaluating open-world uncertainty and model failure. The research architecture is organized around five interconnected layers: versioned biological modeling, explicit prior assumptions and knowledge gaps, physically constrained predictive interrogation, comparative adaptive experimentation, and independent requalification. The manuscript develops thirty candidate mathematical research plates covering Bayesian mechanism inference, conditional information gain, experimental identifiability, observation uncertainty, transport dynamics, calibration, model discrepancy, and decision safety. These mathematical structures are connected to eighty-two research chapters, five independently paginated investigation sections per chapter, two hundred detailed Research Gates, and thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Research Gate is intended as a transferable research question that future investigators may test, challenge, refine, or reject. The proposed evaluation compares twin-guided sampling against optimized fixed schedules, established experimental-design approaches, and alternative active-learning policies under matched physical constraints and experimental budgets. Particular attention is given to blinded mechanism identification, probabilistic calibration, out-of-distribution rejection, specimen integrity, model-version accountability, and explicit stopping conditions. The volume includes DOI-linked methodological literature and a staged nonclinical verification pathway. Scientific status and limitations: This manuscript presents a conceptual methodological research program, not completed experimental validation. Its integrated hypotheses, mathematical proposals, and experimental architectures remain subject to independent technical review and empirical testing. The manuscript does not establish clinical efficacy, diagnostic reliability, therapeutic benefit, or proven superiority of microrobotic digital-twin systems. The work also acknowledges remaining editorial limitations, including recurring methodological language that requires further substantive review before the manuscript can be regarded as a fully refined scientific monograph. The broader purpose of this research is to develop scientific systems that can remain useful even when their initial models are incomplete. Rather than demanding certainty from a digital twin, the proposed framework asks whether future autonomous research tools can become more transparent, corrigible, experimentally accountable, and capable of recognizing the boundaries of their own knowledge. Within the STARLI research continuum, this volume is intended as an evolving research inheritance for future human and artificial-intelligence investigators. Language: English Research Type: Conceptual and Methodological Research Monograph Edition

summary: MICROROBOTIC NOISE SEPARATION ENGINEERING FOR QUANTUM BIOSENSING AT THE LIMIT Mechanical Vibration × Quantum Readout Noise × Causal Spectral Analysis STARLI Research Institute XXIX — Flagship Research Monograph 08 When a microrobotic biosensing instrument produces a cleaner waveform, what evidence distinguishes genuinely improved measurement from a signal-processing procedure that has silently removed the very event being investigated? This research monograph develops a nonclinical, hypothesis-forming framework for microrobotic noise separation, causal spectral attribution, and quantum-enabled biosensing. Its central scientific challenge is to distinguish physical specimen-surrogate fluctuations, mechanical vibration, photon-counting statistics, optical reference instability, and shared instrumental noise without incorrectly attributing unexplained residuals to quantum effects or biological activity. The proposed research architecture combines synchronized raw-waveform acquisition, controlled microrobotic actuation, independent reference measurements, complex cross-spectral estimation, uncertainty quantification, and prospective blinded signal-recovery experiments. The 772-page manuscript contains 82 research chapters, 410 independently paginated scientific investigations, 30 interconnected mathematical research plates, 200 Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Major mathematical investigations address power spectral density decomposition, source cross-correlations, spectral coherence, transfer functions, photon shot noise, low-frequency flicker noise, spectral leakage, mechanical harmonics, lock-in detection, multichannel spectral matrices, identifiability, and uncertainty-aware release decisions. A central falsifiable proposition is that controlled alternating actuation combined with independent phase-locked references may improve the separation of movement artifacts from genuine time-localized signals compared with conventional frequency-only filtering. However, successful noise reduction must be demonstrated without sacrificing true-signal amplitude, timing, spectral content, or scientific traceability. Proposed experiments employ artificial pulse generators, controlled vibration platforms, quantum-enabled optical sensing modules, conventional photodetection systems, and independently calibrated references. Performance comparisons include passive vibration isolation, fixed bandpass filtering, stationary sensing, and longer conventional averaging under matched measurement time, bandwidth, energy, and resource constraints. summary: Amun Code is an open-source parallel simulation code for astrophysical fluids and plasmas. It solves the equations of hydrodynamics and magnetohydrodynamics in two and three dimensions on uniform or adaptively refined Cartesian meshes. Supported formulations include Newtonian flows with isothermal or adiabatic equations of state, and special relativistic hydrodynamics and magnetohydrodynamics. The code uses Godunov-type shock-capturing methods with selectable approximate Riemann solvers, high-order weighted essentially non-oscillatory and monotonicity-preserving reconstruction, and Runge–Kutta time integration. Embedded integrators provide error-based time-step control. Magnetic-divergence errors are controlled through generalized Lagrange multiplier cleaning. Optional viscosity, magnetic resistivity, and stochastic turbulence driving support studies of turbulence, shocks, and magnetic reconnection. Driving options include the Alvelius method and an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. Amun Code is written primarily in modern Fortran and supports hybrid MPI/OpenMP parallelization. Simulation settings are supplied through parameter files, and outputs use native XML/binary or HDF5 formats. AmunPy provides a separate Python interface for reading simulation data. The code is developed by Grzegorz Kowal and distributed under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or later.

summary: When a central bank raises rates, the government's interest bill rises. Whether the extra interest supports domestic demand depends on who receives it. Recent evidence finds this direct fiscal channel of monetary policy was small in the United States before 2020, because long Treasury maturities slowed the pass-through of policy rates to interest costs. We argue that this conclusion does not carry over to the post-2022 tightening. Quantitative easing replaced long-term Treasury debt with overnight interest-bearing reserves, so the consolidated public sector repriced far faster than Treasury maturities suggest, and the price-insensitive official holders that once anchored demand for Treasuries were replaced at the margin by domestic private buyers. Using published Treasury, Federal Reserve and TIC data, we decompose the rise in public-sector interest outflows between 2021 and 2024. Net interest rose by about \$530 billion, three quarters of it due to higher rates rather than more debt. Counting the Treasury and the Federal Reserve together, roughly 57 percent of the increase in public-sector interest outflows reached domestic non-federal holders directly, 27 percent reached them through the Federal Reserve's payments on reserves and reverse repos, whose counterpart was the end of its remittances to the Treasury, and 16 percent went abroad. For the Treasury securities the Federal Reserve held at the end of 2021, quantitative easing made higher rates reach non-federal holders' income roughly two to two and a half times as fast as if the bonds had stayed in private hands. Domestic investors absorbed close to 90 percent of the growth in privately held debt. We discuss what this implies for the potency of rate hikes, for the design of interest on reserves, and for reserve-currency issuers more generally.
title: Who Receives the Interest? Reserve Status, Holder Composition and the Fiscal Channel of Monetary Policy

summary: v1.1.0 — final-prediction revision analyses Release date: 23 October 2026. This is an analysis/code release; no models were trained or rescored for it. Included evidence revision-experiments/09_photo_count_final/ : final SigLIP2 MIL ensemble versus random forest, stratified into 278 one-photo, 127 two-photo and 345 three-photo cases; 10,000 paired case-bootstrap draws, confidence intervals, multiplicity adjustments, raw subgroup scores and a publication figure. revision-experiments/10_test_discrepancy/ : reproduction of seven paired macro ROC-AUC DeLong-type comparisons and the historical permutation tests, with a separate rank-scale sensitivity analysis. The primary raw-score permutation remains non-significant (p=0.089891); the macro DeLong-type p=0.000072328 and rank sensitivity answer different null questions. Modules 07 (chance-anchored AP) and 08 (paired AUC), added after the original v1.0.0 snapshot, are now included in the release alongside modules 09 and 10. Saved predictions and analysis inputs remain tracked in Git. Copy manifests verify the original E1/E2 script and result bytes. The manuscript-workspace copies remain unchanged. Correct model identity and availability The final manuscript predictor is the canonical SigLIP2 MIL ensemble of seeds 42–51, followed by validation-fitted per-condition Platt calibration. Its saved test predictions are artifacts/models/mil/siglip2_so400m/canonical/ensemble/test_predictions.csv and reproduce approximately 0.851 macro ROC-AUC and 0.304 macro average precision on the locked 750 cases. The separately fitted final model and earlier ensembles are different predictors. The Hugging Face public HawkFranklin-Research/pelliscope-siglip2-mil and private HawkFranklin-Research/pelliscope-25class-models-internal repositories contain historical 20 September weights. Their cards were explicitly labeled as earlier versions on 23 October; commit receipts are in v1.1.0-huggingface-receipts.json . No weights were changed or represented as the final ensemble. Final September 27 checkpoints are not included in this code release, and their recovery/upload remains pending. Google Cloud access currently requires renewed authentication; VM contents have not been verified in this release session. Reproduce the new analyses From the repository root, in the project environment: python revision-experiments/09_photo_count_final/analyze.py --code-root . python revision-experiments/09_photo_count_final/plot_results.py python revision-experiments/10_test_discrepancy/verify_tests.py --code-root . These commands use saved predictions only. They require neither model checkpoints nor feature banks. See each module README for sparse-label, subgroup and test-null limitations. No causal advantage from multi-image aggregation or clinical benefit is established by these analyses alone. Archive continuity The previous immutable archive is v1.0.0, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23000066 ; its version-series DOI is 10.5281/zenodo.23000065 . The new GitHub release is intended as the next version of that archive. Do not cite the old version-specific DOI as containing these new modules; verify the new version record before updating a manuscript citation.

summary: AI is becoming pervasive in everyday life, appearing as a visible and constant presence in many aspects of work, education, and personal relationships. It restructures job markets, creates new slop aesthetics, and is forcibly incorporated into almost all digital services with promises of economic growth and efficiency, without any serious reflection on the social and political consequences. But we believe that the situation is not hopeless or settled, no matter how powerful the corporations or systems profiting from AI may appear. The trick is to recognize that democratic levers for change are not given in advance, but must be actively and creatively reimagined. This collection of essays is a survey of where such handles are hiding in the digital age, in places considerably less obvious than a county hearing. In procurement, in a watershed boundary, in a tax treaty almost nobody knows exists, in a benchmark written by users rather than engineers, or in a legal assumption about how technology “works” that is ripe for challenging. None of these were designed as democratic instruments, which is precisely the point. Democracy is presented not as a form of government but a way of living, and as a skill that can be practiced. The authors reflect on an emergent, collective argument about the different meanings and possibilities of “digital democracy from below.” They go beyond the U.S. context to explore distinct but interdependent dynamics of technological politics in places around the world. The collection has five sections: (1) Seeing through the fog; (2) Recognizing the limits of infrastructure; (3) Fighting erasure; (4) Practicing everyday democracy; and (5) Resisting, organizing and re-building. It also offers a roadmap for organizing participatory workshops that can adapted and reused. Contributors (alphabetical order by last name): Rafael C. Alvarado, Brianne Anderson, Nicole West Bassoff, Luã Cruz, Aashka Dave, Nancy L. Deutsch, Laurent Dubois, Joshua Earle, MC Forelle, Matthew Gillikin, Sergio Guillen Grillo, Yujia He, Mar Hicks, Steven L. Johnson, Mona Kasra, Tamara Kneese, Andre Vinicius Leal Sobral, Aaron Martin, Andrew Mondschein, David Nemer, Roya Pakzad, Pedro Augusto P. Francisco, Spencer Phillips, Jess Reia, Karina Ripley, Andrea Roberts, Fernanda R. Rosa, Dhanaraj Thakur, Quito Tsui, Michael Tyrala, Jonathan van Geuns, Yingchong Wang, Megan Wiessner, Rebecca Williams, Bianca Wylie, Caitlin D. Wylie.
title: Digital Democracy from Below: Resisting AI and Techno-solutionism

summary: Learnable Representations (LRs) can fit parametric families of functions to diverse kinds of signals. These emergent neural-native data formats are gathering interest in the scientific community due to their compactness, resolution-agnosticism and amenability to direct neural processing. On the other hand, gigapixel images are becoming increasingly widespread across a variety of scientific, cultural, and industrial domains. In this paper, we present GigaBench, the first benchmark and experimental evaluation focused on deploying LRs with gigapixel imagery. GigaBench includes images collected, acquired, and synthetically rendered across diverse domains, and addresses image compression and super-resolution. We adapt a representative set of LRs, spanning Implicit, Hybrid, and Explicit methods, so as to operate reliably at the gigapixel scale on consumer hardware. Through systematic evaluation across reconstruction quality, model size, compression and inference times, we identify consistent trends across methods and suggest actionable guidance for future investigation.
title: GigaBench: Benchmarking Learnable Representations for Gigapixel Image Compression and Super-Resolution

summary: Diffusion models have become strong priors for solving inverse problems. However, nonlinear inverse problems such as phase retrieval remain challenging when multiple measurement-consistent solutions are distinguishable only by the prior; we call such measurements ambiguous. Existing diffusion-based samplers rely on local approximations during reconstruction. For an ambiguous measurement, these approximations can allow measurement guidance to favor a measurement-consistent mode that is close to a prior-supported mode but is itself not supported by the prior. Evaluation often masks this type of failure by reporting the best-of-$k$ runs, where the best is selected by comparison to the ground truth. We introduce Prior-Consistent DAPS (PC-DAPS), a variant of Decoupled Annealing Posterior Sampling (DAPS) designed to address this failure case by maintaining multiple candidate solutions within a single sampling run. As annealing noise decreases, PC-DAPS prunes and replaces weaker candidates according to their prior consistency, without any ground-truth access. PC-DAPS reduces the incidence of prior-inconsistent samples and improves sample quality on nonlinear inverse problems while preserving sample quality and diversity on linear inverse problems.
title: Beyond Best-of-$k$: Prior-Consistent DAPS for Ambiguous Nonlinear Inverse Problems

summary: Multibeam imaging sonar produces intensity images degraded by coherent speckle and system-induced blur, while clean reflectivity targets are rarely available. Existing despeckling methods often rely on simplified intensity-domain noise models, synthetic clean targets, or blind-spot self-supervision, and typically do not jointly model deblurring and speckle suppression. We propose a physics-consistent self-supervised framework for joint despeckling and deblurring of multibeam imaging sonar. A stochastic coherent image-formation model yields a conditional-mean forward operator that relates latent scene reflectivity to expected intensity through the squared magnitude of the system point spread function. We then use registered multi-frame sonar sequences to train without clean ground truth images, showing that, under an idealized inter-frame conditional-mean condition, the expected paired loss equals the corresponding forward-prediction loss up to a network-independent constant. To stabilize the ill-conditioned inverse problem, we further adapt robust equivariant imaging using stochastic coherent simulation and introduce a paired forward prediction error metric for ground-truth-free evaluation. Experiments on two real multibeam sonar datasets demonstrate a favourable balance between forward-prediction agreement, homogeneous-region speckle suppression, and preservation of visible structural boundaries compared with representative baselines.
title: Self-Supervised Multibeam Sonar Restoration via Coherent Forward Modeling
